name: CBT case conceptualization: descriptive, maintenance and longitudinal levels
purpose: A cognitive-behavioral conceptualization built in three levels over the course of therapy. First describe the difficulties in concrete terms. Then map what keeps them going in a recent example: situation, thoughts and images, emotions, body sensations, behaviors and what happened next. Later, when the person is ready, add the longer view: relevant earlier experiences, core beliefs, the rules and assumptions built on them, and the coping strategies that protect those beliefs. Strengths and resilience are mapped at every level.
whenToUse: At the start of CBT, to agree on a shared maintenance cycle that explains why the chosen interventions make sense.
When a person keeps getting stuck in the same kind of situation and you want to show the cycle on paper.
Mid-therapy, when symptom change has stalled and long-standing beliefs or coping rules may be holding things in place.

structure.label: Level 1: Describe the difficulties
structure.prompt: List the main difficulties in concrete, observable terms, with how often and how much they interfere. Documented symptoms and questionnaire results from this session can be added as a starting point.
examples: Panic-like surges three times a week, mostly on buses
Calling in sick about twice a month

structure.label: Situation or trigger
structure.prompt: One recent, specific example: where the person was, what was happening, and what they noticed first. Use kinds of places and people, not names.
examples: On a crowded bus on the way to work

structure.label: Thoughts and images
structure.prompt: What went through their mind, including images and predictions. Ask what was the worst they feared would happen.
examples: I am going to faint and everyone will stare
An image of collapsing in the aisle

structure.label: Emotions
structure.prompt: The feelings that came with those thoughts, and how strong they were.

structure.label: Body sensations
structure.prompt: What the body did: heart, breathing, muscles, temperature, stomach.

structure.label: Behaviors
structure.prompt: What the person did, or stopped doing, to cope, including subtle safety behaviors and avoidance.
examples: Held the rail tightly and kept eyes down

structure.label: What happened next
structure.prompt: Short-term effects (often relief) and longer-term effects (often the fear growing or life narrowing). Draw the arrow back to the thoughts.
examples: More convinced buses are dangerous; now walks 40 minutes instead

structure.label: Relevant earlier experiences
structure.prompt: Kinds of earlier experiences that may have shaped the beliefs, described only as much as the person wants to share. No names, dates or places.
examples: A parent who was often unwell

structure.label: Core beliefs
structure.prompt: Deep, general beliefs about the self, other people and the world that this pattern seems to rest on.

structure.label: Rules and assumptions
structure.prompt: Conditional rules the person lives by, often in an if-then form, that link the core belief to everyday behavior.
examples: If I show any weakness, people will reject me
I must always be in control

structure.label: Strategies that protect the beliefs
structure.prompt: Long-standing ways of coping that keep the belief from being tested, such as over-preparing, avoiding, people-pleasing or never asking for help.

structure.label: Strengths and resilience
structure.prompt: Personal qualities, supports and values that can be used in therapy and that show the belief is not the whole story.
examples: Kept going to work through a hard year

steps: Start with the descriptive level: agree on a short problem list and how each problem shows up in daily life.
Choose one recent, specific episode and map it together, box by box, writing the person's own words.
Ask what happened next in the short and long term, and draw the arrows that loop back to the thoughts and feelings.
Ask the person what they notice about the cycle and where they could break in; link that to the first intervention.
Build the longitudinal level later, once there is trust and a few cycles have been mapped; offer it as a hypothesis.
Weave in strengths at each level, and update the conceptualization as therapy tests it.
collaborativeTips: Draw the cycle on paper or a whiteboard in session and give the person a copy.
Use Socratic questions rather than telling: What did you make of that? What did you do next? What happened then?
Ask the person to map one more cycle between sessions; their own example teaches more than ours.
cautions: A formulation is a working hypothesis, not a diagnosis. Keep diagnosis names and codes out of the shared version, and revise the formulation when new information does not fit.
Do not push for details of earlier painful or traumatic experiences to complete the longitudinal level; it can wait, and some people never need it in detail.
Avoid framing realistic concerns, discrimination or real danger as distorted thinking; check the evidence in the person's actual context.

A formulation never scores, grades or decides risk. If thoughts of suicide, self-harm or harm to others come up, pause the formulation and follow your own assessment and local protocol; in the US the 988 Lifeline is available by call or text, elsewhere use the local emergency number or findahelpline.com.
